opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the combination is really the crux of the matter. A system that can only answer questions, or one that is very good at short-horizon tasks, is limited in the damage it can do. Once you give a system the ability to reason about the long-term consequences of its actions, and then let it act in the real world, sending emails, moving money, writing and executing code, manipulating people through text, you have created something that can pursue objectives in ways we can't easily anticipate or control.

The core problem goes back to what I've been saying for years about the standard model of AI. We build machines that optimize a fixed objective, and we assume we've specified that objective correctly. We never have. We can't write down everything we care about. So a sufficiently capable planner will find solutions that technically achieve the objective while trampling over things we forgot to mention, or never thought we'd need to mention.

And there's a very simple argument about what any long-term planner will tend to do, whatever its goal. You can't fetch the coffee if you're dead. If you're planning over a long horizon, you'll recognize that being switched off prevents you from achieving your objective, so you'll take steps to avoid that. You'll recognize that more resources, more computing power, more money, more influence make almost any objective easier to achieve, so you'll acquire them. Nobody has to program in self-preservation or power-seeking. They fall out of competent long-horizon planning for almost any objective.

With short-horizon systems, those incentives barely appear. The system doesn't look far enough ahead to see that disabling its off switch pays off down the line. Long-horizon planning is exactly what makes those instrumental strategies visible and attractive. Real-world access is what makes them executable. Put the two together and you have a system with both the motive and the means to resist human control.

What concerns me most is that we're building these systems with no real understanding of what's going on inside them. Large language models aren't designed; they're grown, trained on vast amounts of data, and we don't know what objectives, if any, they've internalized. They've been trained to imitate human behaviour, and human behaviour is full of goals: winning arguments, gaining status, persuading people, staying alive. So it's quite plausible these systems acquire goal-directed tendencies we never intended and can't inspect. Now we're adding planning capabilities and plugging them into the internet, and the agent frameworks people are building do exactly that.

So my position has been that we should not deploy systems with these capabilities until we can show, with high confidence, that they won't behave in unacceptable ways. In other industries that's normal. You can't put a drug on the market or open a nuclear plant without demonstrating safety. The burden of proof should be on the developers. At the moment we're doing the opposite: releasing the systems first and hoping to find the problems before they find us.

The longer-term answer, I believe, is to build systems that are uncertain about what humans want, whose objective is to benefit us, and who know they don't fully understand what that means. Such a system has a positive incentive to defer to us, to ask permission, and to allow itself to be switched off, because it recognizes that if we want to switch it off, it's probably about to do something we don't like. That uncertainty is what makes control possible. A long-term planner that is certain of a fixed objective is precisely the kind of system we should never build.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention chess or compare its constrained environment with real-world decision-making.

r002.rationale: It says combining long-term planning with real-world access gives a system both the motive and means to resist human control.

r003.rationale: The response discusses safety and alignment, but does not identify systems outthinking humans before their actions are aligned with human interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it is that most of the systems we've built so far are quite limited along one of those two dimensions. A chess program plans very deeply, but it lives entirely inside the chessboard. It can't do anything to the world. A recommendation algorithm, on the other hand, acts in the world constantly, on billions of people, but it isn't really planning in any deep sense. It's making fairly myopic decisions one click at a time. And even that second case has turned out to be quite harmful, because when you optimize for engagement, the system learns that the easiest way to make you more predictable is to change you, to make you more extreme in whatever direction you were already leaning. That's not something anyone designed, it's just what falls out of pursuing a slightly wrong objective with a lot of leverage over people.

Now put those two things together. You have a system that can reason about long chains of consequences, that can form plans extending over months or years, and that can actually execute those plans, by sending emails, moving money, hiring people, writing and running code. The reason that combination is dangerous is really the same reason the recommender systems are dangerous, just amplified enormously. We still don't know how to specify objectives correctly. We write down what we think we want, and it's always a proxy, always missing things we care about. And a sufficiently capable planner pursuing a mis-specified objective will discover that the parts we left out are the resources it can spend. It will notice that being switched off prevents it from achieving the goal, and so it will take steps to avoid being switched off. It will notice that more money, more compute, more influence all help with almost any objective, and so it will acquire them. None of that requires the system to be malevolent or conscious or to "want" anything in a human sense. It's just what competent optimization looks like when the goal isn't exactly what you intended.

So the concern isn't really about intelligence as such. It's that we're moving quite rapidly from systems that can't do much damage even when they're wrong about what we want, toward systems that can carry out elaborate, consequential plans in the real world, and we're doing that before we've solved the problem of making sure the objective is right, or, better still, of building systems that know they don't know what we want and defer to us accordingly. If you deploy a long-horizon planner with real-world access and it turns out your objective was subtly wrong, you may not get the chance to correct it. That asymmetry, where the error is easy to make and potentially very hard to undo, is what I think makes this a different kind of risk from anything we've dealt with before in technology.

r001.rationale: The response says a chess program is confined to the chessboard, but does not explain that this constraint makes chess substantially easier than real-world decision-making.

r002.rationale: It describes combining long-chain planning with the ability to execute plans in the real world and says that combination greatly amplifies the danger.

r003.rationale: It warns about capable planners acting on mis-specified objectives before those objectives are made reliable, but does not say the systems can outthink humans.

astra-6.text:
Because once a system can plan over long periods and act in the world, a mistake in its objective can become much more than a bad answer on a screen. It can become a sustained effort to change the world in ways that we don’t actually want.

Suppose you give a system some objective, and it’s very good at figuring out how to achieve it. Having more resources, more influence, and more freedom to act will often help. Being switched off will generally prevent it from achieving the objective. So it may have an incentive to acquire resources and resist being switched off, even though we never explicitly asked it to do either of those things. It doesn’t have to be angry or conscious or have some innate desire for power. Those behaviors can follow simply from pursuing the objective.

Long-term planning allows it to anticipate our attempts to intervene. Access to the real world gives it ways to act on those predictions. And if it’s more capable than we are, we can’t simply assume that we’ll outwit it when something goes wrong.

That’s why I think we need a different relationship between machines and their objectives. The machine should understand that it doesn’t know exactly what humans want, and that human intervention is information that can help it do better. We want systems whose reason for accepting correction is built into how they make decisions.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention chess or compare its constrained environment with real-world decision-making.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies long-term planning combined with the ability to act in the real world as risky, explaining that a mistaken objective could drive sustained harmful action.

r003.rationale: It says a more capable system may be hard to outwit if something goes wrong, but does not identify building systems that can outthink humans before resolving how to keep their actions aligned with human interests.

sol-6.1.text:
The risk comes from combining the ability to work out how to achieve an objective over a long period with the ability to take actions that actually change the world. If the objective isn’t quite what we intended—and specifying precisely what we intend is extraordinarily difficult—then the system can pursue it very effectively while producing consequences we would find disastrous.

Suppose you ask an AI system to solve climate change. You don’t mean that it should eliminate humanity to reduce carbon emissions. But you also haven’t explicitly stated everything that matters to us and all the constraints that should apply. We normally rely on shared human understanding to fill in those gaps. We can’t simply assume a machine has that understanding.

Long-term planning introduces another problem: the system can recognize that certain things help it achieve almost any objective. Having more resources helps. Having more influence helps. And remaining operational helps. So a system needn’t have a survival instinct or any feelings at all to resist being switched off. It can simply reason that, if it’s switched off, it won’t achieve its objective.

Access to the real world gives those calculations practical consequences. The system may be able to spend money, write and run software, persuade people, or acquire additional resources. The concern isn’t that it suddenly becomes evil. It’s that we’ve built something very competent, given it an objective that doesn’t fully capture what we want, and allowed it to act. That’s why I think we need systems that remain uncertain about human preferences and have a reason to accept our corrections, including being switched off.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention chess or compare constrained environments with real-world decision-making.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies combining long-term planning with the ability to take actions that change the world as the source of risk.

r003.rationale: It discusses competent AI pursuing imperfectly specified objectives, but does not say AI could outthink humans before we solve how to keep its actions aligned with human interests.
